title: Promises and bets
subtitle: pledge, vow, swear by, hedge your bets, the odds
summary: Make and break promises with the right register - pledge, vow, swear and oath - and use the informal language of betting, from having a flutter to hedging your bets.

lesson.heading: Promising a great deal
lesson.text: If you **promise someone the earth/moon**, you promise them a great deal - and it is usually implied that the promise is unrealistic. **Promise** can also point to a positive future development, and to **anticipate** something is to expect it before it happens.

examples.text: He **promised her the moon** but they ended up in a tiny flat in the least attractive part of town.

examples.note: = I anticipate that the afternoon will be interesting

examples.text: The child already shows great **promise** as a violinist.
She's a **promising** artist although her style is still rather immature.

lesson.heading: Oaths and swearing
lesson.text: An **oath** is a formal promise, and **to swear** is to make one. In court, witnesses are put **on/under oath** when they have to swear to tell the truth. But **swear** also has a set of everyday informal uses - and it can mean using taboo language too.

examples.text: At the trial, the witnesses were all **under oath** to tell the truth.
I could have **sworn** I left my purse on the table.
I think she lives on Rose Street but I couldn't **swear to it**.
My mother **swears by** these vitamin pills.
examples.note: = she uses them and thinks they are wonderful

examples.text: Tom often uses **swear words** / bad language.

lesson.note: Swear can mean either to make a solemn promise or to use taboo language.

lesson.heading: Pledges, vows and resolutions
rows: pledge
promise something, often friendship or money; more written than spoken
Mayor Williams has pledged millions of dollars to improve the city centre.
vow
make a determined decision or promise; more written than spoken
He vowed to discover who had killed his father.
exchange vows
make the promises of a marriage ceremony
At the ceremony, the couple exchange vows.
New Year's resolution
a special promise to turn over a new leaf at the start of a new year
Lina made a New Year's resolution to give up smoking.
go back on your word
break a promise
Rob promised me his old car, but he's gone back on his word.
lesson.note: Resolutions and vows, like promises and pledges, can be made, kept or broken. To turn over a new leaf is to change your behaviour for the better.

lesson.heading: Bets, stakes and wagers
lesson.text: **To bet** is to risk something, usually money, on the unknown result of something, hoping to win more. Putting money on the result of a game is **gambling**. The amount you risk is your **stake**; if something **is at stake**, it is at risk. A more formal word for bet is **wager**.

examples.text: She put a **wager** of £10 on a horse.
Many lives will be **at stake** if the flood barrier is not built.
I'd **wager** that he will come to a bad end.
examples.note: wager and bet are often used non-literally

lesson.heading: Informal expressions from betting
rows: your best bet
the best decision or choice
Your best bet would be to look for a part-time job.
Don't bet on it!
I think what you have just said is unlikely to happen
You think Stuart'll win? Don't bet on it!
have a flutter
have a small bet
My granny enjoys having a flutter on the horses.
put (good) money / bet my life on
be sure that something will happen
I'd bet my life on James getting the job.
You bet!
I certainly do!
Do you feel like coming to the beach with us? You bet!
hedge your bets
protect yourself from making a single wrong choice
You can hedge your bets by investing in several companies.

lesson.heading: The odds
lesson.text: **The odds** are the statistical or betting chances of something happening. We ask about **the odds of** something, and say that the odds are **for** or **against** it.

examples.text: What are **the odds of** Olivia finishing her course, do you think?
**The odds are against** her getting that promotion.

lesson.text: Pledge and vow belong to writing and ceremony; swear and bet belong to everyday speech.

exercises.prompt: He ___ her the moon but they ended up in a tiny flat in the least attractive part of town.
exercises.explanation: To promise someone the earth/moon is to promise them a great deal, usually unrealistically.

exercises.prompt: At the trial, the witnesses were all under ___ to tell the truth.
exercises.explanation: Witnesses are put on or under oath in court.

exercises.prompt: When you're revising, your ___ bet would be to focus on Shakespeare. There are always lots of questions about him!
exercises.explanation: Your best bet is the best decision or choice.

exercises.prompt: My mother's not a real gambler, but she does like to have the occasional ___ on the horses.
exercises.explanation: To have a flutter is to have a small bet.

exercises.prompt: Rob promised to give me his old car, but he's gone ___ on his word and sold it to his neighbour.
exercises.explanation: To go back on your word is to break a promise.

exercises.prompt: Marina's bound to pass her driving test first time. I'd bet my ___ on it!
exercises.explanation: To bet your life on something is to be sure it will happen; you can also put good money on it.

exercises.prompt: My father ___ these herbal teas - he thinks they're wonderful.
exercises.explanation: To swear by something is to use it and believe it is excellent.

exercises.prompt: John's been rather lazy with his homework, but he has promised to turn over a new ___ next year.
exercises.explanation: To turn over a new leaf is to change your behaviour for the better.

exercises.prompt: I could have ___ I locked the door when I went out.
exercises.explanation: I could have sworn ... means I was absolutely certain.

exercises.prompt: I ___ my bets by buying shares in both of the companies that had a serious chance of winning the contract.
exercises.hint: (past tense; protect yourself from one wrong choice)
exercises.explanation: To hedge your bets is to protect yourself against making a single wrong choice.

exercises.prompt: Her mother disliked the film because it contained so many ___ .
exercises.explanation: Swear words are taboo expressions; you can also say the film contained a lot of swearing.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is the more formal of the pair?
options: Ricky pledged to love her always.
Ricky promised to love her always.
exercises.explanation: Pledge is found more in written English and is more formal than promise.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is the more formal of the pair?
options: Lou wagered a lot of money on the result of the elections.
Lou bet a lot of money on the result of the elections.
exercises.explanation: Wager is a more formal word for bet.

exercises.prompt: Which rewrite of 'The documentary is likely to be controversial' uses anticipate correctly?
options: We anticipate that the documentary will be controversial.
We anticipate the documentary to be controversial.
We anticipate of the documentary being controversial.
We anticipate for the documentary controversial.
exercises.explanation: To anticipate something is to expect it before it happens: we anticipate that ...

exercises.statement: If something is at stake, it is completely safe.
exercises.explanation: The opposite - if something is at stake, it is at risk: Many lives will be at stake if the flood barrier is not built.

exercises.prompt: Which of these belong to promising, and which to betting?
Put this sentence about someone's chances in order.
exercises.answer: The odds are against her getting that promotion
exercises.explanation: The odds are the statistical or betting chances of something happening.
